entities.name: Hananchi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Han'anchi (攀安知) reigned as the final monarch of the Sanhoku (Hokuzan) Kingdom on Okinawa Island, a pivotal figure whose defeat in 1416 marked the beginning of Okinawa's unification under the Chūzan Kingdom. His rule, shrouded in historical ambiguity due to scarce contemporary records, represents the twilight of the Sanzan period, an era of three competing polities—Hokuzan, Chūzan, and Nanzan—vying for control of the Ryukyu archipelago. Appearing in Chinese diplomatic records from 1396 to 1415, Han'anchi's interactions with the Ming Dynasty underscore the importance of the tributary system in legitimizing Okinawan rulers and facilitating regional trade, even as internal strife intensified.

Han'anchi's reign was characterized by a precarious balance of power, with his kingdom centered at Nakijin Castle (also known as Hokuzan Castle) in the northern part of Okinawa Island. Chinese accounts confirm his status as King of Sanhoku, though they offer no details on his lineage or succession from the preceding King Min. His last recorded contact with the Ming court in 1415, followed by the complete cessation of Sanhoku's diplomatic missions, strongly suggests his downfall occurred around 1416. This period witnessed escalating military pressure from the southern Chūzan Kingdom, led by the ambitious Shō Hashi, who systematically dismantled his rivals to consolidate power.

The fall of Han'anchi and the Sanhoku Kingdom was a definitive turning point, directly paving the way for the unification of Okinawa under Shō Hashi. This conquest eliminated the last major obstacle to Chūzan's dominance, effectively ending the Sanzan period and laying the groundwork for the establishment of the unified Ryukyu Kingdom in 1429. Han'anchi's defeat thus represents not merely the end of a single reign, but the collapse of a centuries-old political fragmentation, ushering in an era of centralized rule that would define Okinawan history for over four centuries.
